howto.name: How to check an AI assurance claim

steps.name: Name the standard
steps.text: 42001 is governance, 42005 is impact, 17025 is testing, a benchmark is a score. Do not accept one as evidence of another.

steps.name: Check the body and its accreditation
steps.text: A 42001 certificate should come from a body accredited under 17021-1 and 42006 by a recognised accreditation body; a test report from a laboratory accredited under 17025 for that method.

steps.name: Read the scope
steps.text: Which sites, systems, versions and methods the certificate or report actually covers.

steps.name: Check the date
steps.text: Certificates run three-year cycles with annual surveillance; a test report is a snapshot of one version.

steps.name: Ask what is missing
steps.text: Governance without a test, or a test without governance, is half the picture; a regulator will ask for the other half.

short: ISO/IEC 42001 certificates, 42006 and 17021-1 auditors, 42005 impact assessments, 17025 testing laboratories and benchmark scores each prove something different; this page says what each output does and does not show.
title: AI Assurance Standards
subtitle: Which kind of assurance proves what
body_html:
On this page

  • The question every certificate has to answer
  • ISO/IEC 42001: the management system
  • ISO/IEC 42006 and 17021-1: who may audit it
  • ISO/IEC 42005: the impact assessment
  • ISO/IEC 17025: the testing laboratory
  • Model capability tests and benchmarks
  • What each kind of evidence proves
  • How to read an assurance claim
  • Sources

AI assurance is the business of proving something about an AI system to someone who did not build it. Five standards do most of the work, and they prove different things. A certificate under ISO/IEC 42001 says an organisation governs its AI in a defined way. A test report from a laboratory under ISO/IEC 17025 says a specific system did specific things on a specific day. An impact assessment under ISO/IEC 42005 says someone looked at who the system affects. A benchmark score says a model performed on one test. None of these is the others, and most confusion in the market comes from treating one as if it were all of them.

The question every certificate has to answer

Ask of any assurance claim: what was examined, by whom, against what, and what did they conclude. A management system audit examines documents, records and interviews about how an organisation works. A laboratory test examines a system's behaviour under controlled conditions. An impact assessment examines consequences for people. Each produces a different output, and each output is silent on the other two questions.

ISO/IEC 42001: the management system

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the AI management system standard, the AI counterpart of ISO/IEC 27001 for information security and ISO 9001 for quality. It requires an organisation to define the context and scope of its AI activities, set policy and objectives, assign roles, assess and treat AI risks, run an AI impact assessment process, control the AI lifecycle and its data and suppliers, monitor performance, and improve. Annex A lists 38 controls across nine areas; Annex B explains how to implement them; Annex C lists AI-specific objectives and risk sources.

What a 42001 certificate proves: that an accredited auditor found the organisation's AI management system conforms to the standard at the time of audit, within the certified scope. What it does not prove: that any particular model is accurate, safe, unbiased or lawful. The standard governs the process; it never tests the system. The site's ISO/IEC 42001 page covers the clauses and controls.

ISO/IEC 42006 and 17021-1: who may audit it

A certificate is only as strong as the body that issued it. ISO/IEC 17021-1 sets the requirements for any body that audits and certifies management systems: impartiality, competence, the audit cycle of an initial two-stage audit, annual surveillance and recertification every three years, and how findings are handled. ISO/IEC 42006:2025 adds the requirements specific to auditing AI management systems: the AI competence auditors must have, how audit time is set, and what an audit team must be able to assess about AI risk, data and lifecycle controls.

Accreditation bodies, such as ANAB in the United States and UKAS in the United Kingdom, assess certification bodies against 17021-1 and 42006 and accredit them to issue 42001 certificates. A 42001 certificate from a body that is not accredited for it is a claim by that body alone. The accreditation mark, and the scope statement on the certificate, are the two things to check first.

ISO/IEC 42005: the impact assessment

ISO/IEC 42005:2025 gives guidance on assessing the impact of an AI system on individuals, groups and society: when to assess, how to set the scope, what harms and benefits to consider, how to document and act on the result, and how the assessment fits into the 42001 management system, which requires that such assessments be done. It is guidance, not a certifiable standard, so there is no 42005 certificate; its output is an assessment document.

What it proves: that a structured look at consequences for people was taken and recorded. What it does not prove: that the system is accurate or that the assessed risks were reduced. It is the question a regulator reads under Section 1557 or the EU AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment, and it complements rather than replaces a technical test.

ISO/IEC 17025: the testing laboratory

ISO/IEC 17025:2017 sets the requirements for the competence, impartiality and consistent operation of testing and calibration laboratories. A laboratory accredited to 17025 for AI testing has shown that its methods are validated, its staff competent, its equipment controlled and its results traceable and reproducible. This is the standard behind an evidence-grade test report on a specific system: robustness, accuracy on a defined dataset, bias metrics, security testing.

What a 17025 report proves: the results of the tests named, on the system version tested, on the date tested. What it does not prove: anything about the organisation's governance, or about the system after its next update. Accreditation is per test method, so the report's scope matters as much as the laboratory's name.

Model capability tests and benchmarks

Benchmarks such as MMLU, GPQA or the site's tracked leaderboards measure a model's performance on a fixed set of tasks, usually run by the developer or a research group rather than an accredited laboratory. They are useful for comparing models and worthless as compliance evidence on their own: the test set may have leaked into training, the run is rarely reproducible by a third party, and a score says nothing about the deployment the model ends up in. The site's benchmark pages record scores with their provenance for that reason.

What each kind of evidence proves

EvidenceExaminesIssued byProvesDoes not prove
ISO/IEC 42001 certificateThe organisation's AI management systemA certification body accredited under 17021-1 and 42006Governance conforms to the standard, within scope, at audit timeAny property of any specific model
ISO/IEC 42005 impact assessmentEffects on people and societyThe organisation itself, following the guidanceConsequences were considered and recordedAccuracy, safety, or that risks were reduced
ISO/IEC 17025 test reportOne system's behaviour under named testsAn accredited testing laboratoryThe named results on the tested version and dateGovernance, or behaviour after the next update
Benchmark scoreOne model on one task setUsually the developer or a researcherRelative performance on that setCompliance, safety, or real-world fitness
Conformity assessment under the EU AI ActA high-risk system against Annex III dutiesThe provider, or a notified body where requiredLegal conformity for placing on the EU marketAnything outside the assessed system and version

How to read an assurance claim

When a vendor says its AI is certified, ask which standard, which body, which scope and which date. A 42001 certificate covering a corporate headquarters says nothing about the model a customer is buying. A test report for version 3.1 says nothing about version 3.2. An impact assessment written by the vendor is a statement of what the vendor considered. None of this makes the evidence worthless; it makes it specific, and the specificity is the point. The site's NIST AI RMF page covers the voluntary US framework most organisations use to organise these pieces, and the ISO/IEC 22989 page covers the vocabulary the standards share.
